book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

scenes.title: Same engine. Different navigator.
scenes.claim: Agency describes who chooses the next retrieval action
scenes.narration: Imagine a little search ship crossing a universe of papers. Its engine retrieves records. Its navigator decides where to go next. Chapter twelve separates those jobs. An agent changes how a search is controlled. It does not magically replace the engine beneath it.

scenes.title: A task brief is more than a query
scenes.claim: The brief specifies scope, sources, coverage, limits, and output
scenes.narration: The navigator receives a task brief: what counts as useful, which sources to cover, when to stop, and what to return. It turns that brief into queries and tool calls. A query addresses a retriever. A brief addresses the controller that organises the search.

scenes.title: Fixed: the itinerary is already written
scenes.claim: Changing query content can sit inside a fixed sequence
scenes.narration: A fixed workflow follows a prescribed itinerary: search, expand, search again, then merge. Even pseudo-relevance feedback can fit here. The second query borrows words from the first results, so its content changes. But the next operation was decided in advance. Feedback alone does not establish agency.

scenes.title: Adaptive: choose a prepared branch
scenes.claim: A rule, classifier, or model can select an enumerated branch
scenes.narration: An adaptive workflow looks at the yield and chooses among branches its designers listed. Too few results? Broaden. Too many? Narrow. A model may make that choice. Under this chapter's convention, selecting a prepared branch is still adaptive control. Model involvement alone does not make the itinerary agentic.

scenes.title: Agentic: compose a trajectory while searching
scenes.claim: Task + observations → a model-planned sequence of actions
scenes.narration: An agentic controller plans at least part of a sequence from the task and what it observes. It may revise a query, follow a citation, change source, inspect a record, or stop. Its tools already exist. What it composes during the run is their sequence. These arrangements are landmarks on a continuum.

scenes.title: Every navigator has a flight envelope
scenes.claim: Harness: permitted tools, reachable sources, budgets, and gates
scenes.narration: The harness defines the flight envelope: permitted operations, reachable sources, round limits, budgets, and approval gates. Here, a tool means a callable operation, such as fetching references. It does not mean an entire product. Freedom to plan never creates a capability the harness has not provided.

scenes.title: A polished report cannot reveal the controller
scenes.claim: Control, repeated retrieval, and output format are separate properties
scenes.narration: Now separate the route from the destination. A fixed workflow can write a long report. An agentic search can return only records. Repeated retrieval establishes iteration, while report-shaped output establishes generation. Neither tells us who chose the sequence. Inspect the mechanism before trusting the label on the cockpit.

scenes.title: Agentic RAG is one destination
scenes.claim: Agentic RAG chooses retrieval actions towards a generated response
scenes.narration: Basic retrieval-augmented generation retrieves sources and uses them to write an answer. Agentic RAG lets a model choose retrieval actions while working towards that answer. Agentic search is broader: it can finish with evidence and never write prose. Ask who chooses the next action, and what evidence supports that answer.

scenes.title: The navigator cannot rewrite the engine
scenes.claim: Control changes the sequence; retrieval scoring remains its own mechanism
scenes.narration: Our navigator can choose B M twenty five, dense retrieval, citation traversal, or fusion, if those tools are available. It does not change their scoring functions. Hybrid describes contributing retrieval signals. Multi-stage describes sequential operations. Agentic describes control. A system can have any combination of these independent properties.

scenes.title: Find related papers that were not cited
scenes.claim: Required operation: related candidates minus existing references
scenes.narration: Consider the chapter's uncited-papers task. Find an article, extract its references, retrieve related candidates, then remove candidates already cited. These coloured cards are a schematic set example, not measured papers. Understanding the request is insufficient if the available workflow cannot compare the two sets. More rounds cannot invent that missing operation.

scenes.title: A trace shows the flight, not every possible flight
scenes.claim: Actions taken ≠ all capabilities available
scenes.narration: A trace records the actual flight: searches, sources, returned records, and decisions to continue or stop. It does not reveal the whole menu of operations the system could have used. A missing capability and a badly chosen action can produce the same failure. Ask for both the trace and the tool inventory.

scenes.title: An early omission can steer the next search
scenes.claim: Hypothetical run: selection-bias methods absent from round 1
scenes.narration: For the question, does open access increase citations, imagine the first shortlist emphasises overall citation differences. Selection-bias methods are absent. If later searches only follow those records' terminology and references, they may reinforce the same aspect. This is the chapter's hypothetical trajectory, not a claim that citation searching always misses methods.

scenes.title: Investigate a missing aspect deliberately
scenes.claim: Another query or route can expand the cumulative candidate pool
scenes.narration: An alternative action deliberately searches for selection-bias methods alongside the open-access citation advantage. Suppose it finds relevant papers absent from round one. The cumulative pool expands. A task brief, librarian, or controller could prompt this move. Recovery is possible, but neither the action nor its success is guaranteed.

scenes.title: Stopping is a decision about evidence
scenes.claim: Budget reached or diminishing yield does not establish completeness
scenes.narration: A loop may stop because a round limit or budget is exhausted, because a user interrupts, or because the model decides the evidence is sufficient. Record which happened. A quiet final round does not prove complete coverage. A model's stopping judgement needs an inspectable criterion, especially when missing evidence matters.

scenes.title: Flexibility has a price
scenes.claim: More decisions add latency and cost; repeated runs may differ
scenes.narration: Each extra decision and retrieval round adds latency and cost. Two agentic runs may follow different paths, so keep their actual traces. For a familiar task, a well-designed fixed or adaptive workflow may be the better choice. Flexibility earns its place when the required sequence was not supplied in advance.

scenes.title: A connector exposes operations, not new holdings
scenes.claim: MCP describes callable services; access still depends on entitlements
scenes.narration: The Model Context Protocol describes operations a service offers, their inputs, and their outputs so a model can call them. It can connect a controller to an existing search service. It does not replace that service's index, confer subscription access, or compete with RAG. A better navigator still needs reachable evidence.

episodes.title: Give a failed search a second chance
episodes.subtitle: Recovery and the library's knowledge

scenes.title: Zero results can become useful feedback
scenes.claim: A failed attempt can inform the next retrieval action
scenes.narration: A search returns nothing. For a one-shot system, the interaction may end there. A loop can inspect the failure and choose another attempt. The engine need not become more sophisticated. What changes is whether the search process gives an empty result somewhere useful to go.

scenes.title: No database is called autism
scenes.claim: Chapter demonstration: database discovery over a library index
scenes.narration: In the author's June twenty twenty six demonstration, selected database searches from twenty twenty three zero-result logs were replayed against a library index. One request asked for a database for autism. The problem was granularity: no database was named autism. The user needed sources covering a subject, not another spelling of that subject.

scenes.title: Six synonyms can still miss the right level
scenes.claim: Reported same-index example: one-shot expansion still returned zero
scenes.narration: The compared one-shot natural-language search generated six reasonable variants, including autistic disorder and autism spectrum. It still returned zero. Both searches used the same index. More synonyms for the same narrow concept did not solve this particular database-discovery request. A transformation cannot react to results it never sees.

scenes.title: Change the granularity, then try again
scenes.claim: Autism → psychology, medicine, education, disability
scenes.narration: After seeing the empty result, the loop broadened to psychology, medicine, education, and disability. The chapter reports finding PsycINFO, Education Research Complete, and SocINDEX. The useful move was a change of conceptual level followed by another search. These are reported historical examples, not a live test or a current holdings recommendation.

scenes.title: Recovery can happen over a keyword index
scenes.claim: Feedback and reformulation can help without changing the retriever
scenes.narration: This keyword-endpoint example did not require dense retrieval. A holdings C S V and a smaller model also worked in selected comparisons. Those comparisons do not isolate one cause, and useful retries can be fixed or adaptive too. They support investigating recovery, rather than assuming the biggest model or newest representation is responsible.

scenes.title: Selected examples are not a success rate
scenes.claim: Exploratory evidence: selected 2023 queries, answered with 2026 models
scenes.narration: Keep the limits attached to the result. The examples were selected, not sampled, and newer models answered older queries. The holdings C S V changed how the model received the collection. This was an exploratory demonstration of recovery, not a benchmark proving universal superiority, a success rate, or that recovery requires agency.

scenes.title: The library holds the local map
scenes.claim: Supply current holdings, coverage, entitlements, embargoes, and field quirks
scenes.narration: A model may infer broad subject connections from public information. It cannot reliably infer a newly licensed database, your institution's entitlements, coverage dates, embargoes, or local field quirks. The library supplies that map. Routine discovery may become easier, while maintaining accurate local knowledge and handling specialised requests remain essential work.

scenes.title: Judge the recovery, then inspect the route
scenes.claim: Ask: available tools? actions taken? evidence missed? stopping rule?
scenes.narration: To assess an agentic search, ask what tools were available, which actions ran, what evidence could still be missing, and why the run stopped. Test whether poor queries recover on your own tasks. Agency does not improve the retriever's scoring function. It can improve the search process by giving a failed attempt a second chance.
